item.title: Cape Muroto: UNESCO Geopark and Wild Coast — Guide
item.description: Cape Muroto, at the eastern tip of Kochi, is a UNESCO Global Geopark where you can see the earth being made: this is a coast of rapidly uplifting land, where rock once formed deep beneath the sea has been thrust up to form dramatic shores of folded strata, wave-cut platforms and jagged formations. A walking trail and boardwalks lead among the rocks and subtropical plants, with information on the remarkable geology, while the warm Pacific offshore is rich with marine life.

item.title: Diving & Snorkelling in Kagoshima's Islands — Guide
item.description: The warm, clear seas around Kagoshima’s southern islands — especially Yakushima, Amami Oshima and the Amami archipelago — make the prefecture one of Japan’s finest destinations for diving and snorkelling. Bathed by the warm Kuroshio current, these waters teem with life: vibrant coral reefs, schools of tropical fish, sea turtles, rays and, in places, larger marine life, all in visibility that can be superb. Around Yakushima, divers explore reefs and granite underwater landscapes and often encounter sea turtles, while Amami’s extensive coral reefs and lagoons are a highlight of southern Japanese diving.

item.title: Kashiwajima Island: Coral Reefs and Clear Sea — Guide
item.description: Kashiwajima is a tiny island off the far southwestern coast of Kochi, famous for water of extraordinary clarity — so transparent that moored boats appear to hover above the seabed as if floating in air. Where the warm Kuroshio current meets cooler waters, an exceptional diversity of marine life gathers, and the island is ringed by coral reefs home to a huge variety of tropical and temperate fish. This makes it one of the best places in mainland Japan for snorkelling and diving, with easy access to vivid underwater scenery just offshore.

item.title: Okinawa Diving & Snorkelling Guide: Spots, Trips & Tips
item.description: With warm, gin-clear seas, vast coral reefs and abundant marine life, Okinawa is one of Asia’s great diving and snorkelling destinations. From the dazzling “Kerama Blue” reefs and the glowing Blue Cave off Cape Maeda, to manta cleaning stations and the mysterious Yonaguni Monument, there’s something for every level — including easy trial (“experience”) dives for total beginners and snorkelling trips for non-divers. Operators across the island make it simple to get in the water.

item.title: Diving & Snorkelling in Okinawa: Complete 2026 Guide
item.description: Okinawa is Japan’s diving capital — and for good reason. The Ryukyu archipelago stretches 1,200 km from the main island to Yonaguni on the Taiwan border, encompassing some of the most diverse marine environments in the North Pacific: from shallow coral gardens with sea turtles to deep-water hammerhead shark schools, WWII wrecks, and the infamous “Yonaguni Monument” (an underwater rock formation that may or may not be man-made). Is Okinawa Good for Non-Divers?

item.title: Okinawa Solo Travel Guide: Island Hopping, Diving & Ryukyuan Culture
item.description: Okinawa is exceptional for solo travellers. The island’s safety, ease of navigation, year-round warmth, and the social atmosphere of dive boats and guesthouses create a natural environment for meeting people and going at your own pace. The real reward for solo visitors is the ability to slow down and access Okinawa’s cultural depth — the Ryukyuan history, the local izakaya scene, and the outer islands where group tour infrastructure barely exists.
